Intelligent mobility, technology and cross-border connectivity emerge as new pillars of China–ASEAN cooperation
(Singapore, 27 September 2026) As China and Southeast Asia deepen cooperation in technology, intelligent mobility and cross-border trade, Chongqing is expanding its engagement with ASEAN through “The Great Way” (《大道》), a multinational reporting and research initiative spanning Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia and other ASEAN markets.
Launched by Chongqing Broadcasting Group · THE FIRST SIGHT TV - to mark the fifth anniversary of the China–ASEAN Comprehensive Strategic Partnership, the initiative seeks to document how industrial cooperation, connectivity, standards and people-to-people exchanges are reshaping relations between China and Southeast Asia.
Five reporting teams have departed Chongqing for destinations including Singapore, Thailand and Malaysia, exploring developments along the New International Land-Sea Trade Corridor and the broader networks connecting western China with Southeast Asia.
The initiative began in Bangkok on 21 September with “When Chongqing Meets Bangkok” (渝车出海·遇鉴暹罗), an event bringing together more than 100 representatives from government, business, industry, culture and media.
While Bangkok served as the first destination, the programme forms part of a wider ASEAN journey examining how cities and economies across the region are becoming increasingly connected through trade, technology, manufacturing and cultural exchange.
From Chongqing to Southeast Asia
Located in central and western China, Chongqing has developed into an important centre for manufacturing, logistics and technology.
The city has accelerated the development of its intelligent connected new energy vehicle industry, with the ambition of building an internationally influential ecosystem for intelligent mobility.
This transformation is increasingly extending beyond China.
Changan Automobile, headquartered in Chongqing, entered Thailand in 2023 and subsequently established its first overseas new energy vehicle manufacturing base in Rayong Province.
Production commenced in 2025, with the facility positioned not only to serve Thailand but also to support manufacturing and exports to other ASEAN markets and the wider region.
At the Bangkok event, Chris Wu, Vice President of Changan Auto Sales (Thailand) Co., Ltd., highlighted the technological capabilities of Chinese automakers in responding to ASEAN consumer needs and the importance of market-oriented product development.
The development reflects a broader shift in China–ASEAN economic ties, as cooperation increasingly moves beyond the exchange of finished products towards deeper integration involving technology, manufacturing, supply chains and regional markets.
Singapore's Role in an Increasingly Connected ASEAN
For Singapore, these developments are relevant within the broader evolution of ASEAN's economic and technology landscape.
As a regional centre for trade, finance, logistics, technology and corporate headquarters, Singapore plays an important role in connecting businesses operating across Southeast Asia and international markets.
The growth of intelligent mobility and new energy vehicles across ASEAN is also creating a wider ecosystem extending beyond vehicle manufacturing itself.
Digital infrastructure, artificial intelligence, mobility solutions, financing, logistics, charging infrastructure, data, software and cross-border services are becoming increasingly interconnected as the automotive industry undergoes technological transformation.
This creates a broader regional conversation around how markets such as Singapore can participate in and contribute to the next generation of mobility and China–ASEAN economic cooperation.
“The Great Way” Comes to Singapore
Singapore is among the destinations included in “The Great Way”, THE FIRST SIGHT TV's multinational reporting and research initiative examining connectivity and cooperation between China and ASEAN.
Rather than looking at China–ASEAN relations solely through bilateral trade, the initiative explores how different ASEAN economies contribute distinct capabilities to an increasingly integrated regional ecosystem.
The reporting teams will document areas including industrial cooperation, mutual recognition of standards and people-to-people exchanges among economies connected through the New International Land-Sea Trade Corridor.
The corridor provides an important connection between western China and international markets, creating new possibilities for trade and economic interaction between Chongqing and Southeast Asia.
Singapore's inclusion in the initiative reflects the city-state's place within this wider network of regional connectivity and provides an opportunity to examine how Singapore's strengths in international business, innovation and connectivity intersect with Chongqing's growing industrial and technological capabilities.
Beyond Automobiles: Technology as a New Connector
The Bangkok event demonstrated how the automotive sector is becoming a wider platform for technological and economic cooperation.
As vehicles become increasingly electrified, intelligent and connected, the industry is converging with information and communications technology, digital services and new energy ecosystems.
This convergence creates opportunities for cooperation extending well beyond traditional automotive manufacturing.

A Broader China–ASEAN Story
2026 marks the fifth anniversary of the China–ASEAN Comprehensive Strategic Partnership.
Against this backdrop, “The Great Way” aims to document how relations between China and ASEAN are evolving from conventional trade and tourism towards more multidimensional cooperation involving industry, technology, connectivity, media and culture.
Bangkok represents the beginning of that journey.

For Chongqing, this represents an opportunity to connect its strengths in advanced manufacturing, intelligent mobility and logistics with Southeast Asia.

articles.title: Canada-ASEAN Trade Push: Could Southeast Asia Become a Major New Growth Market for Canadian Energy and Businesses? - kalkine.ca
articles.summary: Canada-ASEAN Trade Push: Could Southeast Asia Become a Major New Growth Market for Canadian Energy and Businesses?  kalkine.ca
articles.full_text:
Key Highlights
- Canada is accelerating efforts to deepen economic ties with Southeast Asia.
- Trade negotiations with ASEAN and the Philippines are reported to be more than 90% complete.
- Ottawa is targeting further progress ahead of Prime Minister Mark Carney’s planned visit to the Philippines in November.
- Energy, LNG, critical minerals, infrastructure and technology are emerging as key areas of potential cooperation.
- Canada is seeking additional export markets as it reduces dependence on any single trading relationship.
- Southeast Asia’s growing energy and digital infrastructure requirements could create opportunities for Canadian companies.
- The strategy could have implications for Energy, Mining, Industrials, Technology, Infrastructure and Financial sectors.
Why Is Canada’s ASEAN Trade Strategy Trending?
Canada is accelerating its economic engagement with Southeast Asia as part of a broader strategy to diversify international trade.
The latest development involves negotiations with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations and the Philippines. Canadian officials have indicated that both negotiations are more than 90% complete, with Ottawa seeking to advance the agreements toward completion later this year.
The initiative comes as Canada seeks to strengthen Supply chains, expand export markets and create new opportunities for Canadian businesses.
For investors, the importance extends beyond trade policy.
Southeast Asia is becoming increasingly important for energy, manufacturing, technology, infrastructure and digital services, creating several potential areas of overlap with Canadian industries.
Why Does Southeast Asia Matter to Canada?
Southeast Asia represents a large and growing economic region with rising energy demand, expanding Manufacturing capacity and rapidly developing digital infrastructure.
For Canada, the region offers an opportunity to diversify exports beyond traditional markets.
The Philippines is particularly relevant because of its growing economy, infrastructure requirements and expanding digital sector.
ASEAN more broadly provides access to multiple economies with different industrial and consumer profiles.
A successful trade framework could therefore create opportunities for Canadian businesses across several markets rather than relying on a single bilateral relationship.
Could LNG Become a Major Canadian Export Opportunity?
Energy is one of the clearest areas of potential cooperation.
Southeast Asian economies rely significantly on imported energy, creating Demand for diversified and reliable supplies.
Canada's growing LNG export capacity on the Pacific coast could provide an opportunity to increase energy shipments to Asian markets.
Canadian officials have highlighted energy as one of the country's major offerings to Southeast Asia, particularly as regional economies seek to improve energy security.
For Canadian energy companies, expanded Asian markets could potentially reduce dependence on North American demand.
The commercial opportunity will depend on LNG prices, shipping economics, terminal capacity and long-term supply agreements.
Why Are Critical Minerals Important?
Critical minerals could become another major component of Canada’s Asian trade strategy.
Canada has significant mineral resources, while Southeast Asian economies are expanding manufacturing and technology industries.
Copper, nickel, uranium and other strategic minerals are increasingly important for electricity infrastructure, batteries, advanced manufacturing and technology.
Canadian Mining companies could potentially benefit from stronger links with Asian manufacturers and investors.
However, resource development requires substantial Capital and infrastructure.
The opportunity therefore extends beyond mining companies to railways, ports, engineering businesses and financial institutions involved in project development.
Could Canada’s Trade Push Help the Mining Sector?
Potentially.
Canadian mining companies have traditionally served global markets, but increasing international Diversification could provide additional customers for Canadian mineral production.
The key issue is whether Canada can move from resource extraction toward a more integrated supply chain.
Processing, refining and transportation capacity could become increasingly important.
If Canada develops stronger relationships with Asian manufacturers, demand could potentially extend beyond raw materials toward processed mineral products.
This would support Ottawa's broader objective of increasing domestic economic value from Canada's resource base.
Why Is the Philippines Important?
The Philippines has several characteristics that make it strategically relevant to Canada's diversification strategy.
The country has a large population, expanding infrastructure requirements and growing demand for energy and digital services.
Canadian officials have also identified potential opportunities involving infrastructure, energy and data centres.
The country's growing technology economy could create opportunities for Canadian companies specializing in artificial intelligence, cloud infrastructure, Cybersecurity and digital services.
For Canadian businesses, the Philippines could therefore become both an export market and a potential Investment destination.
Could Data Centres Become a New Canada-Asia Theme?
Artificial intelligence is increasing demand for data-centre infrastructure globally.
Southeast Asian economies are expanding their digital capabilities, while demand for computing capacity continues to increase.
Canada has expertise in artificial intelligence and technology, creating potential opportunities for Canadian businesses to participate in the broader digital infrastructure ecosystem.
Investment opportunities could extend across software, cloud services, power infrastructure, cooling systems, telecommunications and engineering.
The availability of reliable electricity will also be critical because data centres are highly energy intensive.
What Does Trade Diversification Mean for Canadian Companies?
For Canadian businesses, diversification can reduce dependence on any single export market.
That does not mean replacing existing trading relationships.
Instead, companies can potentially build additional Revenue streams in Europe, Asia and other international markets.
For exporters, having multiple markets can provide greater flexibility when tariffs or regulatory changes affect one destination.
For investors, geographic revenue diversification can therefore become an increasingly important Factor when assessing Canadian companies.
Could Infrastructure Investment Increase?
Greater trade with Southeast Asia would require supporting infrastructure.
Canada needs efficient ports, railways, energy terminals and logistics systems to move products toward international markets.
This creates potential opportunities for infrastructure and industrial companies.
Ottawa has already been emphasizing trade corridors and major infrastructure projects as part of its broader economic strategy.
If Asian trade expands, demand for export infrastructure could increase further.
Could Canadian Banks Benefit?
Canadian financial institutions could be indirectly affected by deeper trade relationships.
Companies expanding into Southeast Asia may require financing, foreign-exchange services, trade finance and Investment Banking support.
Infrastructure and resource projects also require significant capital.
Canadian banks with international capabilities could potentially participate in these activities.
However, the direct financial impact will depend on the scale of new investment and the number of Canadian companies expanding into the region.
What Could This Mean for TSX Investors?
The potential market implications are spread across several sectors.
Energy: LNG producers and infrastructure businesses could gain from additional Asian demand.
Mining: Critical-mineral producers could benefit from stronger relationships with Asian industrial customers.
Industrials: Engineering, equipment and infrastructure businesses could participate in new projects.
Technology: AI, cybersecurity, cloud and digital-infrastructure companies could explore opportunities in Southeast Asia.
Utilities: Data-centre growth could increase demand for reliable electricity infrastructure.
Financials: Banks could support cross-border trade, project financing and corporate expansion.
Transportation: Ports, railways and logistics businesses could benefit from higher export volumes.
What Are the Main Challenges?
Trade agreements do not automatically produce higher exports.
Canadian companies still need competitive pricing, reliable supply, sufficient production capacity and efficient logistics.
Distance is another challenge.
Shipping goods from Canada to Southeast Asia can be more expensive than serving geographically closer markets.
Currency movements, Commodity prices and geopolitical conditions can also affect commercial decisions.
Finally, competition from established Asian suppliers remains significant.
Could the Strategy Reduce Canada’s U.S. Trade Dependence?
Diversification is clearly becoming a larger part of Canada's economic strategy.
The objective is not necessarily to reduce trade with the United States dramatically.
Instead, Ottawa is seeking more options.
Stronger relationships with Southeast Asia could provide Canadian businesses with alternative customers and supply-chain partners.
Europe and Asia are therefore becoming increasingly important components of Canada's international economic strategy.
What Should Investors Watch Next?
Investors can monitor several developments.
First, watch whether Canada and ASEAN complete their negotiations.
Second, monitor progress on the Canada-Philippines agreement.
Third, watch for new LNG supply agreements involving Asian buyers.
Fourth, track Canadian critical-mineral projects linked to Asian customers or investors.
Fifth, monitor infrastructure announcement

articles.title: UK Considers Chinese EV Tariffs During EU Trade Discussions - fuelcellsworks.com
articles.summary: UK Considers Chinese EV Tariffs During EU Trade Discussions  fuelcellsworks.com
articles.full_text:
• The UK government is reviewing its tariff policy on Chinese electric vehicles as London seeks access to proposed “Made in Europe” measures amid reported EU pressure for closer alignment on Chinese EV tariffs.
• Britain does not impose the additional anti-subsidy duties introduced by the EU on Chinese-made EVs, while the UK automotive industry is warning that exclusion from “Made in Europe” measures could put an €80 billion [$94 billion] annual UK-EU automotive trading relationship at risk.
Britain is reviewing its tariff policy on Chinese electric vehicles as it seeks access for UK manufacturers to the European Union's proposed “Made in Europe” industrial measures.
UK Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds said tariffs on Chinese EVs were “under review” and described the government's position as “finely balanced,” with different parts of Britain's automotive industry seeking different approaches.
“We are an export-orientated sector. So clearly, you shouldn’t do anything that risks your export markets, and you always have to take heed of retaliatory action if you put tariffs in place,” Reynolds told Politico at the Labour Party conference in Liverpool.
His comments come as London seeks to ensure British manufacturers are not excluded from the EU's proposed “Made in Europe” measures.
The Financial Times reported, citing people familiar with the discussions, that EU officials have pressed Britain to align more closely with the bloc's trade policy, including by raising tariffs on Chinese vehicles. The reported tariff linkage has not been publicly announced by the European Commission.
The UK did not follow the EU when Brussels imposed additional countervailing duties on battery-electric vehicles imported from China in 2024.
EU duties currently range from 7.8% to 35.3%, depending on the manufacturer, on top of the standard 10% import tariff. Britain has not introduced equivalent additional anti-subsidy duties on Chinese EVs.
The issue has become more prominent as Chinese brands increase their UK market share. Chinese-made vehicles account for around 16% of UK new-car sales this year, according to figures cited in reporting on the EU-UK discussions.
The discussions come as the EU works on its Industrial Accelerator Act and proposed “Made in Europe” provisions.
The legislation is intended to support European production through measures including public procurement and industrial support. Britain is concerned that UK-built vehicles and other products could fall outside parts of the framework.
Reynolds said excluding British industry would not serve the EU's objective of strengthening European manufacturing.
“The Made in Europe push is supposed to be about greater resilience, greater autonomy for European industry in the face of very significant pressures from both the U.S. and China,” Reynolds said. “Now, if that is the objective, it stands to reason that the U.K., that’s the second-biggest economy in Europe, should be a part of that.”
The Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders is also pressing for UK-built vehicles to be included.
Oxford Economics analysis commissioned by SMMT estimates that UK automotive production supports around €24 billion [$28 billion] of spending on EU-produced goods and services, 250,000 EU jobs and significant tax revenues.
The UK-EU automotive trading relationship is worth about €80 billion [$94 billion] annually, according to SMMT. Britain is the EU's largest export market for passenger cars, while the EU is Britain's largest passenger-car export market. The UK is also the largest importer of EU-built automotive components.
SMMT chief executive Mike Hawes said excluding British manufacturers from the proposed measures would reduce demand for EU-made components and affect manufacturers on both sides.
SMMT wants UK-produced vehicles to be treated as “assembled in the EU” for the purposes of the proposed rules.
The UK government has not committed to introducing additional tariffs on Chinese EVs.
Higher duties would bring British policy closer to the EU's approach but could expose UK exporters to Chinese retaliation and affect Britain's efforts to attract Chinese automotive investment.
Reynolds said those considerations are part of why the government regards the decision as finely balanced.

articles.title: Malaysia Deports 1,500 Myanmar Nationals in Defiance of United Nations Safety Warnings - streamlinefeed.co.ke
articles.summary: Malaysia Deports 1,500 Myanmar Nationals in Defiance of United Nations Safety Warnings  streamlinefeed.co.ke
articles.full_text:
The Malaysian government has commenced the deportation of approximately 1,500 Myanmar nationals, proceeding with the repatriation operation despite explicit warnings from the United Nations and numerous human rights organisations regarding the safety of the returnees. The group, which includes children and members of the persecuted Rohingya minority, represents the first phase of a broader agreement to return 5,000 detainees to military-ruled Myanmar.
Defiance of International Appeals
The deportation operation began on Tuesday morning when dozens of buses, travelling under heavy police escort, arrived at the Majlis Perbandaran Manjung stadium. The facility, located near the Lumut naval base in northwestern Malaysia, served as the staging area where migrants were processed before being transported to the nearby naval installation. From the base, the detainees were transferred to Myanmar Navy vessels waiting offshore to conduct the repatriation.
The Malaysian authorities executed the transfer in direct defiance of international appeals and legal challenges. Independent United Nations human rights experts publicly castigated the decision, highlighting that returning migrants to crisis-ridden Myanmar breaches fundamental international protection standards. Previous attempts to deport Myanmar nationals from Malaysia have faced similar legal hurdles, including a Kuala Lumpur High Court order intended to suspend returns pending judicial review. The current administration has bypassed these interventions, authorising the naval transfer without conducting individualized protection assessments for the detainees.
The Repatriation Agreement
The foundation for Tuesday's deportations was established in July 2026, when Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim announced that Myanmar had agreed to take back 5,000 members of the Rohingya community. This rare bilateral repatriation push has prompted severe concern among international observers, given the ongoing conflict in Myanmar following the February 2021 military coup. The agreement demonstrates a functional diplomatic channel between Putrajaya and the Myanmar military junta, an engagement that stands in stark contrast to the broader international community's efforts to isolate the regime.
Malaysian officials have defended the returns as a "voluntary" repatriation programme from immigration detention centres. However, rights groups contest this characterisation, arguing that individuals held in indefinite detention without legal recourse cannot provide genuine consent to return to a conflict zone. The lack of transparent screening processes means that legitimate refugees and asylum seekers may be forcibly returned alongside economic migrants.
Legal and Institutional Context
Malaysia is not a signatory to the 1951 Refugee Convention and lacks a domestic legal framework to recognise or protect refugees. Consequently, the hundreds of thousands of individuals who have fled persecution to seek sanctuary in Malaysia navigate daily life without legal status. They remain highly vulnerable to arrest, indefinite detention, and deportation. According to United Nations estimates, there are approximately 190,000 Myanmar refugees and asylum seekers registered in the country, with the Muslim Rohingya minority constituting roughly two-thirds of that population.
The living conditions for these undocumented populations have deteriorated significantly. The recent repatriation plan was accelerated after authorities detained more than 100 Rohingya individuals who had gathered outside the UN refugee agency's office in Kuala Lumpur. These refugees were seeking institutional help after being threatened with eviction from an informal settlement in the northern state of Penang. Although they were later released after officials confirmed they held valid UN documentation, the incident highlighted the precarious existence of displaced communities within Malaysia.
Operational Parameters and Logistics
| Details of the Myanmar Repatriation Operation |  | 
|---|---|
| Operational Element | Status / Quantity | 
|---|---|
| Target Repatriation Figure | 5,000 individuals | 
| Phase One Deportees | Approximately 1,500 individuals | 
| Processing Location | Majlis Perbandaran Manjung stadium | 
| Embarkation Point | Lumut Naval Base | 
| Transport Mechanism | Myanmar Navy vessels | 
Accountability and Consequences
Human rights monitors warn that the returning populations face severe and immediate dangers upon disembarkation in Myanmar. Organisations including Fortify Rights and Human Rights Watch have documented that deportees are exposed to persecution, torture, armed conflict, and forced recruitment into the military. The decision to return unaccompanied minors and young children to a state experiencing widespread internal violence has drawn particular condemnation.
The deportation strategy also places considerable strain on regional diplomatic relations. By engaging directly with the Myanmar military to facilitate the returns, Malaysia risks signalling an implicit endorsement of the junta's legitimacy. This operational coordination complicates the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) consensus, which has struggled to implement a unified response to the Myanmar crisis. As naval vessels transport the first cohort of 1,500 individuals across the Andaman Sea, the fate of the remaining 3,500 detainees slated for repatriation remains a critical humanitarian concern, testing the limits of international refugee protection norms in Southeast Asia.

Investors will flock to countries and sectors they deem most attractive, so Indonesia must give clear signals regarding the direction of its investment policies.

Brussels told London that joining the EU customs union would be the best way to resolve the issue, the Financial Times reported on September 25, citing people familiar with the matter. The British government continues to rule out that option.
The demand presents Britain with a difficult trade-off: higher tariffs could help preserve British companies' place in European supply chains but may also raise car prices for consumers.
The EU's "made in Europe" policy aims to favor manufacturers within the bloc through subsidies and public procurement to counter competition from China.
Britain is seeking to have its automotive, chemical and energy supply chains included in the framework, amid concerns that domestic companies could be excluded from major EU subsidy programs.

articles.title: Southeast Asia manufacturing gains momentum as Vietnam emerges as regional growth leader - Business Upturn
articles.summary: Southeast Asia manufacturing gains momentum as Vietnam emerges as regional growth leader  Business Upturn
articles.full_text:
Southeast Asia's manufacturing economies are entering a new phase of growth as global companies continue shifting production into the region, with Vietnam emerging as one of the strongest performers.
Manufacturing and technology exports have helped several Southeast Asian economies remain resilient despite higher energy prices, geopolitical tensions and uncertainty surrounding global trade. Vietnam has been a particular standout, recording GDP growth of more than 8% during the first half of 2026 while continuing to attract significant foreign investment.
The trend is strengthening Southeast Asia's position as an alternative manufacturing hub as companies diversify supply chains beyond China. However, the picture is not uniform across the region. Vietnam, Malaysia and Singapore have recorded strong growth, while economies including Thailand and the Philippines have expanded at a slower pace.
Japan is also becoming increasingly connected to this shift. Its ageing population and labour shortages have increased the country's reliance on foreign workers, including migrants from Southeast Asia, creating a separate debate over the economic and social costs of immigration.
Southeast Asia manufacturing benefits from supply chain shift
Manufacturing remains one of the most important drivers of Southeast Asia's economic growth in 2026.
Global businesses have spent years attempting to make their supply chains less dependent on a single country. The strategy is often described as “China plus one,” with companies retaining substantial operations in China while establishing additional production facilities elsewhere.
Southeast Asia has been one of the biggest beneficiaries.
Vietnam has attracted manufacturers across electronics, consumer goods and technology. Malaysia has benefited from demand linked to semiconductors and artificial intelligence infrastructure, while other economies across the region are competing for investment in electric vehicles, batteries and advanced manufacturing.
The Asian Development Bank said economic growth across developing Southeast Asia is now expected to reach 4.7% in 2026, slightly higher than its previous forecast of 4.6%.
However, performance differs considerably between individual economies.
Vietnam and Malaysia have been among the stronger performers. Singapore has also benefited from technology-related activity, while Indonesia's large domestic economy has helped maintain relatively steady growth.
Thailand and the Philippines have faced softer momentum.
That divergence means Southeast Asia is increasingly becoming a two-speed region, with economies exposed to technology, manufacturing and stronger exports outperforming countries dealing with weaker domestic demand or slower investment.
Vietnam GDP growth stands out in Southeast Asia
Vietnam has become one of the clearest examples of the region's manufacturing-driven expansion.
The country's GDP increased 8.39% year over year during the second quarter of 2026, according to Vietnam's National Statistics Office.
That pushed economic growth for the first half of the year to 8.18%, compared with 7.63% during the same period in 2025.
Industry and construction expanded 9.81% during the first six months, while services grew 8.09%.
Manufacturing has played an especially important role.
Vietnam's industrial production index increased 10.8% during the first half of 2026. Manufacturing output alone expanded 11.4%, making it one of the biggest contributors to overall industrial growth.
Foreign investment has added another source of momentum.
International companies continue to use Vietnam as a manufacturing base for products ranging from electronics and consumer devices to machinery and components.
Investment is also beginning to move into more advanced areas.
Industrial and technology parks around Ho Chi Minh City are attracting projects connected to artificial intelligence, data centres, digital infrastructure and high-tech manufacturing.
Vietnam is therefore attempting to move beyond its traditional position as a relatively low-cost manufacturing destination and capture more valuable parts of global technology supply chains.
The Asian Development Bank recently raised its forecast for Vietnam's 2026 GDP growth to 7.8%, up from its previous estimate of 7.2%.
The bank also increased its 2027 forecast to 7.6%.
Vietnam faces challenge of turning manufacturing boom into long-term growth
Vietnam's rapid expansion does not mean its economic outlook is without risks.
Its manufacturing model remains heavily dependent on foreign investment and international demand. A slowdown in major export markets could therefore affect factories and employment relatively quickly.
The United States is Vietnam's largest export market, while China remains its largest source of imports.
That leaves Hanoi exposed to changes in global trade policy.
Vietnamese leader To Lam said this month that negotiations with the United States over a trade agreement had made substantial progress and could be approaching a final outcome.
A stable agreement would be particularly important for Vietnam because of the country's reliance on exports.
There are also domestic challenges.
Rapid credit growth, higher energy prices and stronger consumer demand could increase inflationary pressure. The Asian Development Bank expects Vietnamese inflation of around 4.3% in 2026.
Infrastructure must also expand quickly enough to support the country's manufacturing ambitions.
Factories require reliable electricity, ports, roads and logistics networks. Vietnam will need significant investment in all of these areas if it wants to maintain rapid industrial growth.
The country's longer-term objective is even more ambitious. Hanoi wants to achieve sustained high growth as Vietnam moves towards high-income status.
Doing so would require the economy to gradually shift from labour-intensive production towards industries that generate greater productivity and value.
Japan immigration debate grows as labour shortages deepen
Southeast Asia's changing economic role is also becoming increasingly connected to Japan's demographic problems.
Japan has one of the world's oldest populations and has struggled with a declining workforce.
Businesses in sectors including construction, agriculture, manufacturing, hospitality and elderly care increasingly depend on foreign workers to fill vacancies.
Many of those workers come from Southeast Asian countries such as Vietnam, Indonesia and the Philippines.
That has created an economic contradiction.
Japan needs additional workers to support industries facing severe labour shortages, but a larger foreign population also creates costs for language education, administration, housing and integration.
Local governments can face additional spending as communities adapt to a more internationally diverse workforce.
The debate is therefore no longer simply about whether Japan should accept foreign workers. The more difficult question is how the country can design an immigration system that provides the workers its economy requires while ensuring communities and migrants receive adequate support.
For Southeast Asian workers, Japan can offer higher wages than those available in their home countries. Remittances can then provide income for families and communities across the region.
Japan, meanwhile, gains access to a younger workforce that can help keep businesses operating as its domestic working-age population shrinks.
Southeast Asia could gain bigger role in Asian economy
The manufacturing shift, Vietnam's rapid GDP growth and Japan's dependence on overseas workers all point towards a broader change in Asia's economic structure.
Southeast Asia is no longer simply competing for basic factory production.
Countries across the region are increasingly trying to attract semiconductor investment, data centres, electric-vehicle supply chains, artificial intelligence infrastructure and other higher-value industries.
Vietnam's recent numbers demonstrate the opportunity. Its economy expanded more than 8% during the first half of 2026, manufacturing remained strong and foreign investment continued flowing into industrial projects.
But the region's performance remains uneven.
Higher energy costs, trade tensions, extreme weather and weaker global demand remain important risks. The ADB has also warned that geopolitical conflicts could push commodity prices higher and weigh on economic activity across Asia.
Vietnam will now be closely watched to see whether it can maintain its manufacturing momentum through the remainder of 2026.
The larger story is not simply that factories are moving into Southeast Asia. The region is gradually becoming more important to global supply chains at the same time that ageing economies such as Japan increasingly depend on Southeast Asia for workers. If those trends continue, the region's role in the Asian economy could become substantially larger over the coming decade.

articles.title: Thailand AI Exports Break 56-Month Record on Pre-Sold Hard Drives and PCBs - Tech Times
articles.summary: Thailand AI Exports Break 56-Month Record on Pre-Sold Hard Drives and PCBs  Tech Times
articles.full_text:
Thailand's outbound shipments surged 24.3% year-on-year in August to US$34.62 billion — the fastest growth in 56 months — and the two technologies driving it are already spoken for years into the future. The country supplies roughly 80% of the world's hard disk drives and has become the primary Southeast Asian hub for printed circuit boards engineered specifically for Nvidia AI servers, and both product categories are producing order books that stretch well past this year. That combination makes the record monthly data released Friday by Thailand's Commerce Ministry something more than a trade statistics beat: it is a concrete, monthly-updated measure of how fast the global AI infrastructure buildout is actually proceeding.
Why Thailand Is Winning the AI Hardware Race
Electronics account for roughly one-third of Thailand's total export value, and the sector delivered outsized gains in August. Industrial-product exports climbed 27.1% for the month, logging their 29th consecutive year-on-year increase.
The individual component figures tell the hardware story in granular terms. Video-recording equipment and components rocketed 1,155.7%, a surge explained by the rapid deployment of AI-powered surveillance and network video recorder systems globally, each of which requires both high-bandwidth image-processing chips and high-capacity HDD storage for raw video data. Telephones and components rose 151.2%, printed circuits surged 126.8%, electrical transformers and parts climbed 55.6%, and computers and components — a direct bellwether for data-center buildout — rose 42.1%.
"The strong performance is partly driven by global AI investment, which has created insatiable demand for the hardware components Thailand specializes in manufacturing," Nattiya Sujinda, deputy director of Thailand's Trade Policy and Strategy Office (TPSO), told reporters Friday in Bangkok.
What AI Server PCBs Actually Are — and Why Thailand Makes Them
The most consequential technical shift inside Thailand's electronics sector is the transformation of its printed circuit board industry. A standard server PCB has 10 to 16 layers of circuitry. An AI server PCB — the kind that connects Nvidia GPUs in training and inference clusters — requires 24 to 46 layers, uses ultra-low-loss M8-grade resin laminates instead of the commodity FR4 fiberglass that dominated the industry for decades, and demands thermal and power management systems capable of handling GPU loads in the hundreds of watts per chip. These are fundamentally more sophisticated products, and Thailand is now making them at scale.
The supply chain connection to Nvidia is direct. Victory Giant Technology — Nikkei Asia's identified top Nvidia PCB supplier for AI servers and graphics cards — has opened its second factory in Thailand, in Ayutthaya, 60 kilometers (37 miles) north of Bangkok, and is ramping new equipment. Gold Circuit Electronics, a key PCB supplier for Nvidia switch trays (the components that connect GPUs in high-density clusters), is running its first Thai facility at full capacity. More than 60 PCB companies have established or expanded operations in Thailand in recent years, including the majority of the world's top-tier PCB makers.
"Any suppliers that are involved in the AI supply chain are leading the formation of the Thailand PCB industry," a manager at Ta Liang Technology, a drilling-machine provider that serves all of the top PCB makers, told Nikkei Asia.
The financial scale of this transformation is significant. Thailand's Board of Investment (BOI) confirmed that the country has attracted more than 200 billion baht (approximately US$6 billion at current exchange rates) in PCB investment applications since 2022 and has emerged as ASEAN's largest printed circuit board manufacturing base.
Hard Drives: The Quiet Engine Nobody Expected AI to Revive
If AI server PCBs are Thailand's new story, hard disk drives are its old story with a stunning second act. Seagate and Western Digital together operate manufacturing facilities that account for roughly 80% of the world's HDD supply, with both companies' primary final-assembly operations based in Thailand. This was supposed to be a sunset industry: consumer PC demand for HDDs had been declining for years as solid-state drives became cheaper.
AI changed the math. Cloud hyperscalers building out AI training infrastructure require enormous volumes of high-capacity nearline storage to hold training datasets, model checkpoints, and inference logs — workloads where HDDs remain dramatically cheaper per terabyte than flash storage. The result: Western Digital CEO Irving Tan disclosed on the company's Q2 FY2026 earnings call that the company's entire 2026 HDD capacity sold to its top seven cloud customers, with long-term allocation agreements extending into 2027 and 2028. Cloud revenue now accounts for 89% of Western Digital's total.
Seagate told investors the same story in its Q2 2026 earnings call: nearline capacity fully allocated through calendar year 2026, with long-term agreements in place with major cloud customers through 2027. Both companies have announced Thailand capacity expansions in response to renewed demand. Western Digital is in the process of a 23 billion baht Thailand expansion (approximately US$693 million) at its Bang Pa-in and Prachinburi facilities approved by the BOI.
This sold-out status — both producers, both committed to HDD production through at least late 2027 from Thai facilities — is what gives August's export data its structural character. The shipments that produced the 24.3% August headline were not a demand surprise; they were the fulfillment of contracts already signed with the world's largest hyperscale cloud operators.
United States Dominates Demand
The United States has been the dominant driver of this year's growth, and August was no exception. Thai exports to the US surged 48.7% year-on-year, marking the 35th consecutive month of year-on-year gains. Electronics components — the building blocks of AI accelerator hardware and data centers — feature prominently in those shipments.
The tariff context matters here. Effective July 24, 2026, the US imposed an additional 12.5% Section 301 levy on most Thai exports, related to US concerns about Thailand's forced-labor import rules. The levy is higher than the 10% rate applied to ASEAN peers such as Indonesia and Malaysia that have signed Agreements on Reciprocal Trade with Washington, and Bangkok is actively seeking parity. But the 12.5% rate is not as damaging to the AI hardware story as it might appear: integrated circuits and hard disk drives are among more than 2,120 Thai products explicitly exempted from the additional levy. The products at the heart of the AI buildout shipments — the ones driving 48.7% US-bound export growth — are largely not subject to the tariff.
There is, however, a live risk. A separate US Section 301 investigation into excess industrial capacity — involving Thailand and 15 other countries — is still underway, with tariff rates not yet announced. Thailand's prime minister was expected to raise the issue directly with US President Donald Trump in a phone call around September 17 or 18; as of Friday, no deal on a reciprocal trade framework had been concluded.
China Demand: Durians and Data
On the China front, the August rebound was driven not by semiconductors but by tropical fruit. Chinese demand for fresh durian and mangosteen from Thailand's southern provinces surged, helping agricultural exports return to growth for the first time in four months, with the category rising 4.2% year-on-year. Agricultural and agro-industrial exports combined rose 1.4%.
Thai exports to China climbed 15.5% year-on-year in August, adding to a broader market-diversification story. Shipments to the European Union rose 23.1%, Japan gained 19.6%, and Australia jumped 81%.
Does the Boom Have Structural Legs?
The IMF's July 2026 World Economic Outlook identified Thailand alongside Taiwan, South Korea, and Malaysia as one of the world's four leading net exporters of AI-related hardware — a category that covers computer equipment and components, semiconductor-manufacturing machinery, and processors and memory chips. The BOI subsequently recorded US$43.6 billion (approximately 1.47 trillion baht) in foreign and domestic investment applications during the first half of 2026 alone, a 37% year-on-year surge, with the digital sector accounting for US$33 billion of that total.
Since 2023, Thailand has attracted more than US$26.8 billion in investment applications in semiconductor and advanced electronics specifically, spanning 880 high-tech projects. Major electronics companies operating in the country now carry order books stretching three to five years ahead.
Thailand's data-center investment pipeline provides the self-reinforcing backdrop. According to Cushman & Wakefield's Asia Pacific Data Centre Investment report, Thailand is positioned to attract approximately US$15.9 billion (570 billion baht, approximately US$17.2 billion at September 2026 exchange rates) in data-center investments between 2026 and 2030, as hyperscale providers seek alternatives to Singapore's increasingly constrained land and power resources. Pre-leasing activity has expanded ninefold year-on-year. Every data center built on Thai soil in this pipeline represents additional demand for the PCBs and HDDs that Thai factories already make — a demand loop that reinforces the export figures.
Narit Therdsteerasukdi, BOI Secretary-General and the architect of Thailand's national semiconductor strategy, has framed the goal explicitly: Thailand needs to move beyond assembly into higher-value activities across the AI, semiconductor, and advanced-electronics supply chain. The National Semiconductor and Advanced Electronics Board finalized a strategy in January 2026 targeting more than 2.5 trillion baht (approximately US$75 billion) in semiconductor investment by 2050, with immediate priority on power, senso

articles.title: FDI flows fuel growth of Vietnam’s industrial property market - LuatVietnam
articles.summary: FDI flows fuel growth of Vietnam’s industrial property market  LuatVietnam
articles.full_text:
As ring roads, metro lines and airport connectivity infrastructure are gradually completed in the coming years, demand for housing, industrial property, retail space and hotels is expected to expand beyond traditional urban centres.
Steady growth in foreign direct investment (FDI) is driving the development of Vietnam’s industrial property market while strengthening the country’s position in global supply chains. As FDI enterprises in electronics, optical products, computers and high-tech industries expand production and supply chains in Vietnam, demand for industrial land, factories and warehouses is rising accordingly.
Policies strengthen investor confidence
According to the National Statistics Office, disbursed FDI in the first eight months of 2026 was estimated at US$ 17.25 billion, up 12 per cent year-on-year and the highest eight-month figure in five years. Processing and manufacturing remained the dominant sector, attracting US$ 14.24 billion, or 82.6 per cent of the total.
While Vietnam’s appeal was once largely attributed to labour costs, land availability and geographical location, it is now increasingly underpinned by an industrial ecosystem capable of meeting the stringent requirements of multinational corporations. Key advantages include an open policy environment, improving inter-regional transport connectivity and a growing supply of quality industrial property.
Nguyen Phuoc Thuan, Director of Industrial and Office Leasing at Cushman & Wakefield Vietnam, said investors today are looking beyond attractive opportunities and competitive commercial conditions, with increasing attention being paid to investment transparency, policy stability and the ability of authorities to coordinate and support projects throughout implementation.
The Government is continuing to introduce policies to create a favourable investment and business environment for FDI enterprises. Politburo Resolution No. 10-NQ/TW, dated June 8, 2026, on the development of the foreign-invested economic sector, is seen as a positive signal that strengthens international investor confidence and demonstrates the Government’s commitment to supporting foreign investors.
The resolution sets strategic orientations for attracting a new generation of FDI, focusing on high technology, innovation and sustainable development. It also calls for an integrated investment ecosystem linked with capital markets, international financial centres, free trade zones, economic zones, industrial parks and logistics infrastructure, alongside pilot mechanisms with outstanding institutional frameworks to attract high-quality capital while controlling risks.
Meanwhile, the amended Investment Law and Decree 96/2026/ND-CP continue to improve the investment environment towards greater transparency, convenience and competitiveness.
The draft Investment Law further eases market-access conditions and reduces barriers and compliance costs for foreign investors while maintaining the principles of openness, transparency and consistency.
Savills Vietnam said FDI’s impact on the property market extends beyond the industrial segment. New investment generates demand for jobs, offices, housing, retail space, hotels and serviced apartments, creating spillover effects across multiple property segments.
Savills also noted major investments in education, healthcare and energy infrastructure, helping diversify the economy’s growth base. Against this backdrop, industrial property most clearly reflects the combined impact of FDI and connectivity infrastructure.
Inter-regional connectivity upgraded comprehensively
Infrastructure and transport networks are being extensively planned and upgraded nationwide, strengthening regional connectivity and logistics capacity, a key factor directly supporting industrial property.
In the south, the Ho Chi Minh City People’s Committee is seeking feedback on the master plan for the city for 2025-50, with a 100-year vision, with multimodal network of expressways, strategic ring roads such as Ring Roads 3 and 4, the Ben Luc-Long Thanh and Ho Chi Minh City-Moc Bai expressways, national and high-speed railways connecting industrial parks, seaports and airports, as well as seaports, inland container depots and integrated logistics centres.
These developments are creating a more favourable operational foundation for industrial projects.
In the north, Dong Anh, Me Linh and Soc Son are envisioned as a driving force for international integration and centres for services, trade, logistics and high-tech industry linked with Noi Bai International Airport. Key metro lines, including Lines 2, 10 and 14, are being developed, while the completion of Ring Road 4 and the expansion and upgrading of Noi Bai Airport, together with logistics centres and international free trade zones, are expected to strengthen the region’s position on the national production and logistics map.
According to Avison Young Vietnam, the shift of global supply chains into Vietnam is accompanied by increasingly demanding requirements for infrastructure quality and operational readiness. Businesses are seeking not only land but also complete technical systems, from power and water supplies to logistics and supply-chain connectivity.
As land availability gradually becomes more limited in some key markets, the development of modern, multi-storey factories and warehouses is emerging as a natural solution to maximise land-use efficiency.
According to Thuan, this trend is consistent with the orientation of Resolution 10-NQ/TW, as Vietnam shifts from simply attracting capital towards projects with higher technological content, greater added value and higher operational standards.
Vietnam’s growth story is about not only the pace of growth but also where growth is taking place and how effectively growth centres are connected.
As ring roads, metro lines and airport connectivity infrastructure are gradually completed in the coming years, demand for housing, industrial property, retail space and hotels is expected to expand beyond traditional urban centres.
Locations with strong connectivity will have an advantage in attracting residents, businesses and investment capital. At the same time, new economic corridors could accelerate the development of urban and commercial centres, reshaping the property value map in key localities and across the wider region.
 
 - (VNA/VLLF)

articles.title: The Morowali Nickel Processing Complex Is Polluting Indonesia’s Clean-Tech Workforce - Earth Island Institute

articles.full_text:

EVERY MORNING, BEFORE he opens his eyes, Iqbal already knows what kind of day awaits him. If it rained overnight, the air carries a grudging freshness. If it didn’t, the morning belongs to sulfur fumes.
Iqbal, 20 — who, like his classmates, asked to be identified by a pseudonym to protect his career prospects — lives with three roommates in a fifth-floor student dormitory at Labota Village in Bahodopi, a district in Indonesia’s Morowali Regency, Central Sulawesi. Little more than a decade ago, the area was a quiet landscape of fishing villages and forest. Today, the sprawling Indonesia Morowali Industrial Park (IMIP), the world’s largest nickel-processing complex, runs right up to the walls of his school, the Morowali Metal Industry Polytechnic.
“At first, looking at the environment, I couldn’t stand it. But you start to get used to it.”
This proximity means that, each morning before breakfast, Iqbal and his housemates tackle their daily cleaning routine: sweep the lobby, wipe the hallway, clean the floors outside the rooms. Because the windows in their dormitory room do not seal completely, gray dust rising from the industrial zone constantly enters their living space, settling on every surface.
“If you wear a black hoodie and ride your motorbike for just five kilometers around Bahodopi,” Iqbal says, “by the time you arrive, your hoodie isn’t black anymore. It’s gray.” A sixth-semester student, he speaks about pollution the way other people speak about weather — as a condition of the place, not as a crisis within it. “At first, looking at the environment, I couldn’t stand it. But you start to get used to it. It just becomes your everyday life.”
His classmate Raka, also 20, grew up in Morowali, and remembers the dense forests and nearly impassable dirt roads that used to define the region before industry took over. “People used to say, ‘Why would anyone go to Morowali? It’s just jungle,’” he recalls.
Now, Morowali sits at the center of the global EV supply chain. The 2,000-hectare Indonesia Morowali Industrial Park has swallowed the forests, reshaped the local coastline, and blanketed surrounding communities with industrial pollution. Just beyond the industrial park stands the Morowali Metal Industry Polytechnic, built to prepare a generation of Indonesian students for “green energy” jobs in the industry that is poisoning them.
MOROWALI’S TRANSFORMATION began with Indonesia’s downstreaming policy that banned the export of raw nickel ore. Leveraging the country’s vast nickel reserves — the largest in the world — the strategy effectively forced foreign companies to build their processing smelters on Indonesian soil, reshaping the region with remarkable speed. Since construction on IMIP began in 2013, the industrial park has attracted more than $34.3 billion in investment and grown into a 5,500-hectare complex of more than 50 tenant companies. Today, nearly 90,000 workers smelt nickel ore, process EV battery chemicals, manufacture stainless steel, and operate the coal plants that keep the industrial park running.
The boom has made Morowali Indonesia’s wealthiest regency by gross regional domestic product per capita. But many residents say the prosperity has largely bypassed them. According to a 2023 analysis by the environmental advocacy group Action for Ecology & People’s Emancipation, about 95 percent of the wealth generated in Morowali flows elsewhere. As the report’s lead author, Arianto Sangadji, recalls hearing from a local community member: “We only get the dust.”
The industrial park has, however, created tens of thousands of jobs. To ensure those jobs went to trained Indonesians — and to meet the industry’s massive demand for skilled workers — the government and industry built a polytechnic school right beside the factories.
The Morowali Metal Industry Polytechnic was established in 2015 after IMIP donated around 30 hectares of land for the campus, and Indonesia’s Ministry of Industry financed its construction. The school was designed as a workforce pipeline. Government officials and industry executives co-designed the curriculum, which focuses on just three majors — mechanical maintenance, mineral chemical engineering, and electrical installation engineering — all tailored to the needs of the industrial park.
A boat heads toward a fishing village in north Morowali where stilt houses perch over the water. Little more than a decade ago, the area where the industrial park now sits was a quiet landscape of fishing villages and forests. Photo by Marwan Mohamad / Wikimedia Commons.
Since then, the 2,000-hectare Indonesia Morowali Industrial Park has swallowed the forests, reshaped the local coastline, and blanketed surrounding communities in industrial pollution. Photo by Tom Hegen.
Today, the polytechnic enrolls more than 600 students, and graduates around 100 each year after four semesters of classroom instruction, followed by a year-long industrial internship. Nearly all go on to work at IMIP. According to the school’s 2025 tracer study, 99 percent of graduates found employment, with 87 percent securing jobs immediately after graduation. In a July 2025 interview with the Indonesian daily Pikiran Rakyat, the polytechnic’s director, Agus Salim Opu, described graduates as effectively “sold out” to meet the industrial park’s overwhelming demand.
The industry-school relationship extends beyond curriculum design and graduate recruitment. The industry supplies half of the school’s teaching staff and fully funds tuition for every student. In classrooms, in addition to technical skills, students are taught that they are preparing to power the global green energy transformation. Every morning, however, they wake up surrounded by the pollution that makes that transformation possible.
TO PROCESS THE nickel required to build the world’s “clean” energy future, Indonesia has embarked on one of the largest expansions of coal-fired power on earth. IMIP alone relies on around 20 captive coal plants — off-grid power stations built within and immediately around the complex exclusively to supply the industrial park — with a combined capacity exceeding 5,500 megawatts. Their emissions drift across Bahodopi, settling as the fine gray dust that students find inside their dormitories and classrooms.
Iqbal articulates the contradiction. “In the places using electric vehicles, the area is safe — green energy, no pollution,” he says. “But here, where the materials are made… We are the ones sacrificing our land.”
“The air has become like a poison for the body. It’s like a ticking time bomb.
And, increasingly, their health. A 2024 study by the human rights and environmental nonprofit TuK Indonesia and researchers at Tadulako University found that acute respiratory infections treated at Bahodopi’s community health center skyrocketed from just over 10,000 cases in 2020 to more than 55,000 in 2023. Measurements of particulate matter (PM10 and PM2.5) and sulfur dioxide in villages surrounding the industrial park routinely exceed Indonesia’s national health standards.
“The air has become like a poison for the body,” Raka says. “It’s like a ticking time bomb. You might not feel it immediately, but if you keep living here, it will almost certainly damage your respiratory system.”
Pollution in Morowali extends beyond the air. For his final thesis, Raka is researching ways to maximize the efficiency of high-pressure acid leaching. This is one of the key refining processes used to produce battery-grade nickel. But the process creates a devastating byproduct: millions of tons of toxic tailings. Today, vast tailings facilities, visible even from satellite imagery, occupy hillsides across Central Sulawesi, looming over the rivers that nearby communities depend on for drinking water and agriculture.
Despite all of this, the polytechnic’s core curriculum does not formally require classes in environmental mitigation. “Material about environmental impacts and mitigation efforts is very important,” Iqbal says, reflecting on what is missing from their foundational studies. “It can increase awareness and responsibility for the surrounding environment, supporting sustainable development in Bahodopi.” Neither IMIP nor the polytechnic responded to requests for comment regarding the omission of these subjects from the degree program.
Environmental health experts argue this educational gap leaves students vulnerable. Kiki Sanjaya, a public health researcher at Tadulako University who coauthored the 2024 air quality study, notes that integrating topics like air quality index monitoring and extreme weather preparedness into the syllabus is crucial. “The main goal is not to avoid all exposure — which is impossible — but to build risk literacy,” Sanjaya explains. “This allows students and graduates to recognize hazards, understand risk levels, and protect themselves using evidence-based practices.”
Instead, Raka says the instructors regularly present their own version of environmental reality. He remembers a day in 2025 when a lecturer affiliated with an IMIP tenant company presented results from air-quality tests conducted inside the park, claiming compliance with national health standards. The students, who had commuted through the smog that morning, sat in their chairs and said nothing. “Our reaction wasn’t to argue; it was more like shock,” Raka recalls. “With what we experience every day, we just couldn’t believe it.”
But they understood that they shouldn’t speak up. They are, after all, being trained to work at IMIP.
WHILE THEY CANNOT change the air they breathe in their dorms, the students do everything they can to be there for one another. As head of education and training for the student association, Iqbal spends part of every week helping new arrivals survive the transition. He tells incoming students what he wishes

articles.summary: Indonesia's processed nickel output grew more than 60-fold by 2023  intellinews.com

Indonesia produced 41% of the world's processed nickel in 2023, up from 1% in 2014, according to Our World in Data.
Indonesia overtook China as the world's largest producer of processed nickel in 2021. Source: Our World in Data, based on BGS World Mineral Statistics (2025), CC BY.
Production rose from around 22,000 tonnes in 2014 to more than 1.4mn tonnes in 2023, according to a data insight published by Our World in Data, based on British Geological Survey figures. Indonesia overtook China as the largest producer in 2021 and was well ahead by 2023.
Jakarta encouraged domestic processing by banning exports of unprocessed nickel ore, betting that miners would build smelters at home rather than lose access to the world's largest reserves of a metal used in stainless steel and electric-vehicle batteries.
Indonesia first banned ore exports in 2014 under its 2009 mining law, relaxed the ban in 2017 and reinstated it in full from January 1, 2020, according to a US International Trade Commission working paper. Export bans, along with planned windfall taxes and export levies on nickel and coal, remain at the core of the government's resource nationalism as it hunts for new revenue.
Chinese investment helped finance the expansion. Chinese companies own the vast majority of Indonesia's nickel refining assets, the International Energy Agency (IEA) said in its Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2025. The report said Indonesia hosted almost 45% of global refined nickel production but Indonesian companies accounted for only 10% of global production by ownership, while Chinese firms controlled 65% of global output by ownership against 30% by location, the agency calculated.
The Indonesia Morowali Industrial Park on Sulawesi, heavily financed by China's Tsingshan Holding Group, is the centre of the industry, though its growth has been marred by pollution and unsafe labour conditions, as well as clashes between Chinese and Indonesian workers.
The reciprocal trade agreement Indonesia signed with the US in February has raised questions about access to battery materials, given China's dominant position in Indonesian nickel refining.
Jakarta is now pushing state companies further down the chain. State-owned miner Aneka Tambang (IDX: ANTM) is developing $3.3bn of nickel processing plants in East Halmahera, according to a September 10 presentation cited in the linked report. Its partners include battery maker CATL (SZSE: 300750), while a separate project involves Zhejiang Huayou Cobalt (SHA: 603799).
An August 24 report put Indonesia's share at more than 60% of global nickel output, alongside efforts by Western-backed investors to secure alternative supplies in countries such as Tanzania. The measure is distinct from the processed-nickel series above.

articles.title: ASEAN urged to deepen investments as ‘China+1’ shift deepens China reliance - Manila Bulletin
articles.summary: ASEAN urged to deepen investments as ‘China+1’ shift deepens China reliance  Manila Bulletin
articles.full_text:
The Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) should deepen investments within the region to develop another source of growth as its export-driven economies become increasingly caught between Chinese supply chains and Western demand, according to the Institute of International Finance (IIF).
In two reports last Monday, Sept. 28, the Washington-based global financial industry association said the so-called “China+1” strategy, under which companies diversify manufacturing and supply chains beyond China, has often resulted in “more China through different channels” rather than reducing Southeast Asia’s reliance on the world’s second-largest economy.
“ASEAN is gaining manufacturing activity and exporting more to the United States (US), but this expansion in part relies on Chinese intermediate inputs, capital goods, and value added,” the IIF said.
In 2025, ASEAN accounted for 18 percent of China’s exports and 14 percent of its imports, while China accounted for 14 percent of ASEAN exports on top of 29 percent of its imports, the IIF noted. China’s exports to ASEAN have risen by more than 50 percent over the past four years and by 175 percent since the US imposed substantial tariffs on Chinese goods during the first Trump administration.
China’s trade surplus with ASEAN exceeded $300 billion in 2025, equivalent to more than 6.5 percent of the region’s gross domestic product (GDP). ASEAN also posted a $202-billion manufacturing trade deficit with China but a $317-billion manufacturing surplus with the rest of the world, the IIF’s reports showed.
The Philippines has likewise become more integrated into China-linked production networks, with IIF data showing that Chinese value added accounted for 8.6 percent of Philippine gross exports in 2022, nearly triple the 2.9 percent recorded in 2010.
Across ASEAN, China’s contribution to the region’s gross exports increased to 11 percent in 2022 from 4.7 percent in 2010. “ASEAN’s manufacturing ascent is therefore extending China’s production networks more than displacing them,” the IIF said.
China has also expanded investments in ASEAN, with the region accounting for 53 percent of its outbound direct investment flows and 27 percent of its investment stock in 2024, excluding offshore financial centers. More than one-third of China’s investment stock in ASEAN was in manufacturing, up from one-sixth a decade ago, data showed.
The IIF noted that China’s involvement in the Philippines, Indonesia, Laos, and Malaysia has focused mostly on mining and infrastructure, where overseas contracted projects exceeded outbound direct investment.
In the Philippines, the IIF cited Manila’s decision to drop Chinese funding for three railway projects after financing stalled “amid a broader deterioration in China-Philippines diplomatic relations” during the current Marcos Jr. administration.
Financial links are also deepening, with 34.9 percent of ASEAN-China goods trade settled in renminbi in 2024. The Philippines is among six ASEAN economies with renminbi clearing banks, alongside Cambodia, Laos, Malaysia, Singapore, and Thailand.
A total of 150 financial institutions across ASEAN participate in China’s Cross-border Interbank Payment System (CIPS), which processed ¥21 trillion worth of cross-border payments between China and ASEAN in 2024, double the amount a year ago, the IIF noted.
However, the IIF warned that this growing interdependence leaves ASEAN more exposed to trade as well as geopolitical tensions between China and the US, raising the need to develop additional sources of growth from within the region.
The IIF said ASEAN’s manufacturing trade deficit with China widened by $160 billion over the past two years, while its manufacturing surplus with the rest of the world increased by a similar amount.
Intra-ASEAN trade, meanwhile, declined from about 25 percent of the region’s total trade two decades ago to slightly above 20 percent in 2025, even as its value roughly tripled, as differences in income and productive capabilities continue to constrain trade among member economies.
The IIF’s trade complementarity index showed that the Philippines’ import needs had the strongest match with exports from Malaysia among the economies covered, with an index of 44.5, followed by Singapore at 39.8, South Korea at 39.4, Thailand at 38.5, and China at 36.4.
This index stood at 29.8 for Japan, 26.9 for Indonesia, and 25.7 for Vietnam, reflecting the IIF’s broader finding that ASEAN economies in many cases have stronger trade complementarity with China, Japan, as well as South Korea than with fellow ASEAN members.
As such, the IIF identified investment as a more promising near-term avenue for deeper regional integration. “Intra-ASEAN investment may be the more plausible next frontier,” it said, noting that foreign direct investment (FDI) could help build productive capabilities, internationalize ASEAN firms, and mobilize regional savings.
Intra-regional investment has expanded more slowly than investment from outside ASEAN and remains heavily concentrated in Singapore, while inward investment from China, Japan, as well as South Korea is now as large as intra-ASEAN FDI, the IIF noted.
The IIF said greater intra-ASEAN investment could mobilize more of the region’s savings as well as support the emergence of ASEAN-based regional firms, complementing rather than weakening the region’s investment and trade links with China, Japan, South Korea, and global markets.

articles.title: Foreigners’ unauthorized installation of giant ball on Vietnam rice terrace draws backlash - Tuoi Tre News | The News Gateway to Vietnam
articles.summary: Foreigners’ unauthorized installation of giant ball on Vietnam rice terrace draws backlash  Tuoi Tre News | The News Gateway to Vietnam

articles.full_text:
Mu Cang Chai, a popular mountainous destination in Pung Luong Commune, is home to jaw-dropping terraced rice fields.
The large black ball completely covered the iconic round terraced plot, disrupting the natural beauty of the golden rice season.
Pham Hoang Cuong, a photographer from Hanoi, said he was shocked to see the unusual ball while taking photos of the terraced fields.
Multiple tourists and photography enthusiasts were present at the site at the time, and several voiced their objections.
Cuong approached the foreigners and asked them to remove the ball, saying it disrupted the scenery.
“This could have been an art project,” Cuong said.
“The foreigners said they had obtained permission from the field owner, paid an entrance fee, and rented the spot to place the ball.
“They also said they planned to leave it there for only a few days, but dismantled it later due to a backlash."
The black-ball installation was removed after about two hours.
According to local authorities, officials went to inspect the site after receiving information but found that the foreigners had already left.
Ho Thi De, vice-chairwoman of Pung Luong Commune's administration, confirmed that no permission was sought or granted to install an artwork on the terraced fields.
She stressed that the commune will not approve similar projects, as they damage the heritage landscape.
According to local residents, visitors are charged VND25,000 (nearly US$1) per person to enter the iconic round rice terrace for sightseeing and photography.
Tourists pay to admire the pristine beauty of the terraced fields during the harvest season, and any artificial installation undermines the experience.
Several witnesses said they did not understand the purpose behind placing the rubber ball there.
Local resident Tran Ngoc Linh emphasized, “The terraced fields and mountains of northwestern Vietnam are already beautiful. Please keep them original. Modern art belongs in public spaces, not heritage landscapes.”
According to the Vietnam National Authority of Tourism, Mu Cang Chai’s terraced rice fields cover about 2,200 hectares, with 330 hectares recognized as a national heritage site by the Ministry of Culture, Sports, and Tourism in 2007.
In 2019, the terraced rice fields were recognized by the prime minister as a special national heritage site.
The area is known for its terraced landscapes and two particularly scenic seasons, including the flood season in April and May and the harvest season in September and October.
